Apart from Ilam in the far east, these districts are found west of Kathmandu. For the Bote 
portion of fieldwork, Nawalparasi and Chitwan districts were visited. 
Majhi and Bote communities are often located along riverbanks. In each of the communities 
visited, there is a river either directly accessible for daily use or visible from a distance. Many Majhi 
communities in Kavre, Ramechhap, and Khotang are positioned along the Sunkoshi River, Tamakoshi 
River, and Dudhkoshi River respectively. Bote communities in Nawalparasi and Chitwan are near the 
Narayani River and Chitwan National Forest. 
1.2 Languages 
The 2011 National Census (Central Bureau of Statistics 2014) reports 24,422 mother -tongue Majhi 
speakers among the 83,727 ethnic Majhi people living in Nepal. The name ‘Majhi’ means ‘fisherman.’ 
The Majhi language [mjz]
2 is classified by the Ethnologue as Indo-European, Indo-Iranian, Indo-
Aryan, Outer Languages, Eastern, Bihari (Eberhard et al. 2023). 
There is significant lexical and grammatical variation reported within Majhi (Dhakal 2014). 
Detailed information on the Tamakoshi variety of Majhi spoken in Ramechhap, and some 
comparative work done on this variety and the Sunkoshi and Dudhkoshi varieties spoken in Kavre 
and Khotang respectively, is provided in a grammar of Majhi (Dhakal 2014). 
Information used in the following sections of this report originates from geographical sites found 
within these three dialects (Dhakal 2014): Tamakoshi, Sunkoshi, and Dudhkoshi. Limited information 
is also provided in this report on the sub-dialects of the Tamakoshi variety.
3 
The 2011 National Census reports that, of the 10,397 ethnic Bote people within Nepal, 8,766 
speak Bote as their mother tongue (Central Bureau of Statistics 2014). The Bote language [bmj] 4 is 
classified by the Ethnologue as Indo-European, Indo-Iranian, Indo-Aryan, Outer Languages, Eastern,

Unclassified (Eberhard et al. 2023). The name for the Bote language is reported to have been 
bestowed by an outsider and may have been derived from the English word ‘boat’ (van Driem 2001: 
1172). The Ethnologue lists Bote-Majhi as one of the alternate names used for Bote (Eberhard et al. 
2023). 
Limited information on dialects within the Bote language is available. Gautam and Thapa -Magar 
(1994) report that it “is seen that Bote of one area speak a slightly different language than the Bote 
of another area”. Toba (2002) notes that there is regional variation within Bote and identifies Bote 
varieties by the name of the district they are spoken in. 
This study looks at two of the main dialects of Bote. The following sections include information 
on the Bote variety spoken in Nawalparasi and the Bote variety spoken in southern Chitwan.  
1.3 Peoples 
Majhi people are traditionally fisherman with their lifestyles closely tied to river systems found 
throughout the eastern hills of Nepal. Dhakal (2014) outlines three stories of origin told by Majhi 
people. According to one story, Lord Mahadeva was requested to create Majhi people for the purpose 
of river ferrying. Some Majhi people believe they are descendants of Kus, the son of Ram, from the 
Ramayana, an ancient Hindu epic poem. Others believe Majhi people are the descendants of 
Vyasdeva and Majhini. Bista (1967) adds that some believe Majhi people are descendants of the 
Rajputs who migrated to Nepal from India at the time Muslims were entering India. However, he 
suggests that Majhi people are likely native to Nepal and dwelled in Nepal long before the Raj puts 
migrated into Nepal. 
Bote people are traditionally boat ferrymen and fishermen. The lifestyles of Bote people living 
close to the river systems of Nepal can still be tied to both traditional occupations. There are fewer 
known postulated stories of origin for the Bote people. However, Bista (1967) believes it is likely that 
Bote people are some of the original inhabitants of Nepal.

1.4 Literature on Majhi and Bote 
While there is a good deal of research available on the Majhi and Bote cultures and languages, it is 
important to understand that Majhi and Bote have at times been portrayed as the same group of 
people in literature pertaining to them. Views differ on the relatedness of their speech varieties with 
sources sometimes referring to both speech varieties as the same language. This section will explore 
some of these different perspectives in relevant literature on Majhi and Bote in order to clarify the 
outcomes of this survey. 
From one perspective, Majhi and Bote people are presented as the same group with a shared 
language. Bista (1967:140) states, 
Majhi is actually a term used by the hill peoples for those people called ‘Bote’ in the Terai … 
They are also occasionally referred to as Kushar. All are identical, Majhi, Bote and Kushar; 
they speak one language and follow the same patterns of life. 
In his culture sketch, Bista (1967:142–143) refers to ‘Majhi’ people throughout and uses the 
term ‘Bote-Majhis of the Terai’ as a type of regional term for some Majhi people. 
Van Driem (2001:1172) portrays the Majhi and Bote people in the same way: 
Majhi and Bote are two names for the same population group … The Majhi living in the Terai 
are called Bote, whereas the term ‘Majhi’ is applied to the same ethnic group living upstream 
in the hills. Some members of this group in Tanahun district even refer to themselves as ‘Bote 
Majhi’. 
However, van Driem (2001) further explains that there has been little study on dialectal 
variation within the Majhi language (in which he includes speech varieties referred to in this study as 
‘Bote’). 
In some cases, previous research on one group of people was performed in areas discovered in 
the current study to be primarily associated with the other group of people. For example, in their
